tagline: Company stores and miners’ homes follow the valleys of coal country.
intro: The Coal Heritage Trail crosses rugged mountains and follows streams and rivers on roads that are often narrow and curving. Small commercial districts occupy the valleys, while residential areas climb the steep mountains. The Federal Highway Administration identifies this National Scenic Byway with the coal industry’s effects on the land and on society, pointing to company towns, railroad structures and reclaimed mining land along the corridor. The West Virginia byways guide describes a two-lane highway through this industrial landscape.

Mining jobs brought people from many lands into southern West Virginia. Changes in the industry later left deserted mines and remnants of company towns beside stores, clubhouses and courthouses crafted by Italian stonemasons. The road received national scenic byway designation in 1998. At Beckley, one mine had already taken on an educational role: commercial operations ended in 1953, and the exhibition mine opened in 1962. Its restored passageways and vintage track preserve part of the working environment.

For a southbound drive, follow the corridor from Ansted through Beckley and Mullens toward Welch. Itmann lies between Mullens and Pineville, off WV 16. At Welch, the trail changes to US 52 for the journey toward Bluefield. Bramwell, beside the Bluestone River, is connected by US 52 to Bluefield to the south.

moments.title: Itmann
moments.text: Itmann’s company store and office forms a sandstone complex arranged around an open courtyard. Architect Alex B. Mahood designed the building, constructed in 1923–1925 to serve the mining community. The complex has four sections, including a one-story loggia, with taller gabled sections flanking the courtyard. The town preceded it: Pocahontas Fuel Company built 120 dwellings near Barkers Creek in 1916 and opened the mine in 1918. Its name compresses the company president’s initials and surname, I. T. Mann. The store survives, but the town account describes it as empty after part of it served as a homeless shelter.

moments.title: Kimball
moments.text: Kimball is the site of the first war memorial building erected in memory of African-American veterans of World War I. The town incorporated in 1911 and took its name from railroad official Frederick J. Kimball. It lies on the Norfolk Southern network, formerly the Norfolk and Western.

moments.title: Bramwell
moments.text: Large houses built by wealthy coal operators distinguish Bramwell on the Bluestone River. Coal camps multiplied in the surrounding region during the 1880s, and the town was established in 1888. The town’s prosperity did not spare its downtown from a major fire in January 1910, when 21 buildings burned. Many houses have early-twentieth-century designs. A local museum concentrates on coal and railroad history, two subjects central to the local account. The town entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1984. US 52 passes through its eastern side, with Pinnacle Rock State Park just southeast.
